title: Mamertines
capsule: The Mamertines were Campanian mercenaries who had served Agathocles, Tyrant of Syracuse; they took their name from Mamers, the Oscan war-god. In 288 BCE they treacherously seized Messana (modern Messina) by massacring its male inhabitants and seized control of the Strait of Messina, from which they raided Sicilian settlements and disrupted coastal shipping for two decades. Around 270 BCE they suffered a major defeat at the Longanus River at the hands of Hiero II of Syracuse, after which they simultaneously appealed to Carthage and to Rome for protection — the resulting competition between those two powers escalated into the First Punic War (264–241 BCE), one of the most consequential conflicts of antiquity. Their independent political role disappeared as they became absorbed into Roman Sicily following Rome's victory.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Their control of Messana is well-documented in ancient sources (Polybius, Diodorus Siculus), but the extent of their raiding territory beyond northeastern Sicily is not precisely delimited.
